tabs.title: Day 1
tabs.text:
DAY 1 | DAYID 3050201 | STARTER | Build a Game from Shapes
LEARNING TARGET: I can recognize TurboWarp's stage, sprites and code tools because simple reusable shapes help me test a new interactive design.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(A): Break a real-world problem into smaller parts using a flowchart.
50-MINUTE RHYTHM: 4 min Warm-Up; 13 min Group Learn with live teacher demo; 7 min Group Practice/prediction; 6 min independent DAILY evidence; 15 min project build/test; 5 min save/TEKS Temperature/Studio as appropriate. Shrink activities before rushing or making assumptions about previous class completion.
WARM-UP (participation; full key 305020109998): What can a plain square tell a player about a game without any artwork? Choose one movement you would expect.
GROUP LEARN / HOOK: Today we design a tiny falling-objects game before any story or artwork. The STAGE is where the game happens; each SPRITE is an independently controlled object; COSTUMES change appearance; CODE scripts give instructions; the green flag starts events. The x-axis is left/right (−240 to 240) and y-axis up/down (−180 to 180). Drawing tools: choose Paint a Sprite, select rectangle or circle, choose fill/outline and make one large clear shape; avoid detailed costumes. Name the square Player and circle FallingObject, and leave background plain. The shapes are temporary placeholders, not final art.
GROUP PRACTICE: Teacher demonstrates selecting sprites, painting a 40×40 square and circle, naming them and confirming that clicking one sprite changes its code workspace. Students narrate each click and identify Stage versus Sprite pane before doing it independently.
DAILY MASTERY STUDENT QUESTION — FULL KEY 305020130059: A student puts the player square and falling circle in ONE sprite. Explain why two separate sprites would make coding easier and identify one test proving the objects are controlled separately.
PINNED HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 accurate, specific and independently justified with a feasible test; 70–89 Explains independent sprite code and describes a real test of separate behavior; 50–69 partially correct, missing important detail or validation; below 50 insufficient/contradictory evidence. Missing/unsubmitted is a separate nonnumeric state under RTS-02.
INDEPENDENCE: The question is answerable from TODAY'S teaching and examples without requiring the actual game to work or reference to an unfinished artifact. At most ONE short typed answer field; accessible optional selections may support it. Submit through the shared capture-first two-button Form workflow; no fabricated receipt.
PERFORM / PROJECT DEVELOPMENT: Save ONE named TurboWarp project (Falling Objects — first draft). Create Player as a square and FallingObject as a circle using simple built-in drawing tools. Select each separately and change its position so both appear on the stage. Reopen or relaunch the saved file to confirm the shapes remain. No decorative drawing and no working fall required today.
CREATIVE STUDIO (one required participation zone, separate Xtra; student's choice using same taught tools): Try a larger player shape; compare circle/square readability; sketch three alternative worlds on paper without changing sprites.
TEKS TEMPERATURE CHECK: thumbs for today's skill plus optional specific confusion. Separate Xtra, not part of DAILY mastery or Major.
END-OF-DAY SAVED EVIDENCE: Two named placeholder sprites exist and save correctly.
NEXT DAY PREPARATION: Keep original file; do not start a second game or replace placeholder sprites until Part 2.

tabs.title: Day 2
tabs.text:
DAY 2 | DAYID 3050202 | LEARN | Make the Player Move
LEARNING TARGET: I can connect events, loops and position changes because repeatable controls make interactive objects predictable.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(D): Work together on a flowchart showing a problem, solutions and a development timeline. §126.18(c)(1)(F): Explain why repeating code or steps can make an algorithm useful.
50-MINUTE RHYTHM: 4 min Warm-Up; 13 min Group Learn with live teacher demo; 7 min Group Practice/prediction; 6 min independent DAILY evidence; 15 min project build/test; 5 min save/TEKS Temperature/Studio as appropriate. Shrink activities before rushing or making assumptions about previous class completion.
WARM-UP (participation; full key 305020209998): Which arrow key should move the square toward the right side of the screen, and how would you check?
GROUP LEARN / HOOK: An EVENT starts a script; a FOREVER loop repeats checks; CHANGE X changes horizontal position. The teacher projects and models this exact Player script: when green flag clicked → go to x:0 y:−125 → forever {if key [right arrow] pressed? then change x by 8; if key [left arrow] pressed? then change x by −8; if x position > 215 then set x to 215; if x position < −215 then set x to −215}. Students observe how each block is located in Events, Motion, Control, Sensing and Operators. A restart must reset the same position each time.
GROUP PRACTICE: Teacher drags one block at a time while class predicts outcome: green flag resets position; right key increases x; left decreases x; boundaries prevent disappearing. Students arrange a paper block-flow sketch before implementing.
DAILY MASTERY STUDENT QUESTION — FULL KEY 305020230060: The player is at x=0 and must move right when a key is held. Name the relevant event/loop and x-change behavior, then describe how you would test that the green flag resets the player.
PINNED HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 accurate, specific and independently justified with a feasible test; 70–89 Names event and repeating input/motion steps and proposes a valid reset test; 50–69 partially correct, missing important detail or validation; below 50 insufficient/contradictory evidence. Missing/unsubmitted is a separate nonnumeric state under RTS-02.
INDEPENDENCE: The question is answerable from TODAY'S teaching and examples without requiring the actual game to work or reference to an unfinished artifact. At most ONE short typed answer field; accessible optional selections may support it. Submit through the shared capture-first two-button Form workflow; no fabricated receipt.
PERFORM / PROJECT DEVELOPMENT: Select Player only. Build the displayed reset-and-forever keyboard control. Test right, left, both stage edges, and stopping/restarting. Leave FallingObject untouched. Save the SAME project; do not duplicate it.
CREATIVE STUDIO (one required participation zone, separate Xtra; student's choice using same taught tools): Try a slower value and explain the effect; compare two keyboard speeds; invent a player-friendly controls hint.
TEKS TEMPERATURE CHECK: thumbs for today's skill plus optional specific confusion. Separate Xtra, not part of DAILY mastery or Major.
END-OF-DAY SAVED EVIDENCE: Square moves right and left, stays visible and resets on restart.
NEXT DAY PREPARATION: Keep original file; do not start a second game or replace placeholder sprites until Part 2.

tabs.text:
DAY 3 | DAYID 3050203 | PERFORM | Make the Circle Fall Forever
LEARNING TARGET: I can use repetition and random positioning because a game needs repeatable behavior with changing challenges.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(F): Explain why repeating code or steps can make an algorithm useful. §126.18(c)(2)(A): Change and rename variables, and describe the kinds of data they store.
50-MINUTE RHYTHM: 4 min Warm-Up; 13 min Group Learn with live teacher demo; 7 min Group Practice/prediction; 6 min independent DAILY evidence; 15 min project build/test; 5 min save/TEKS Temperature/Studio as appropriate. Shrink activities before rushing or making assumptions about previous class completion.
WARM-UP (participation; full key 305020309998): If y decreases as a circle falls, what happens after it passes the bottom edge?
GROUP LEARN / HOOK: The falling script belongs to FallingObject, not Player. Exact teacher recipe: when green flag clicked → forever {go to x:(pick random −210 to 210) y:170; repeat until (y position < −175) {change y by −5; wait 0.03 seconds}}. Forever restarts the drop; repeat until ends an individual fall; random x varies each start. Keep its sprite a plain circle. Compare one loop that repeats the entire game and another loop that controls one falling trip. Change the speed cautiously and test from a known reset.
GROUP PRACTICE: Teacher predicts output for fixed x versus pick random, demonstrates sign of negative y, then changes only one parameter. Class identifies loop nesting and why a sprite script must be attached to the correct object.
DAILY MASTERY STUDENT QUESTION — FULL KEY 305020330061: A circle falls correctly once and then stops. Explain what a forever loop and a reset near the top accomplish, and how random x changes the next round.
PINNED HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 accurate, specific and independently justified with a feasible test; 70–89 Correctly explains repeated falling, top reset and controlled random starting x; 50–69 partially correct, missing important detail or validation; below 50 insufficient/contradictory evidence. Missing/unsubmitted is a separate nonnumeric state under RTS-02.
INDEPENDENCE: The question is answerable from TODAY'S teaching and examples without requiring the actual game to work or reference to an unfinished artifact. At most ONE short typed answer field; accessible optional selections may support it. Submit through the shared capture-first two-button Form workflow; no fabricated receipt.
PERFORM / PROJECT DEVELOPMENT: Use the exact supplied FallingObject recipe, test at least five drops, verify the player still responds, and save SAME project. Keep a simple scoreboard note listing observed spawn x changes, fall direction and restart behavior.
CREATIVE STUDIO (one required participation zone, separate Xtra; student's choice using same taught tools): Compare two safe falling speeds; test fixed versus random starting x; sketch an optional second falling-object type without coding it.
TEKS TEMPERATURE CHECK: thumbs for today's skill plus optional specific confusion. Separate Xtra, not part of DAILY mastery or Major.
END-OF-DAY SAVED EVIDENCE: Player moves independently while the circle repeatedly falls from changing x positions.
NEXT DAY PREPARATION: Keep original file; do not start a second game or replace placeholder sprites until Part 2.

tabs.title: Day 4
tabs.text:
DAY 4 | DAYID 3050204 | PERFORM | Lives, Hits and Fair Rules
LEARNING TARGET: I can apply detection, variables and testing because a playable game needs fair consequences and clear feedback.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm. §126.18(c)(2)(A): Change and rename variables, and describe the kinds of data they store.
50-MINUTE RHYTHM: 4 min Warm-Up; 13 min Group Learn with live teacher demo; 7 min Group Practice/prediction; 6 min independent DAILY evidence; 15 min project build/test; 5 min save/TEKS Temperature/Studio as appropriate. Shrink activities before rushing or making assumptions about previous class completion.
WARM-UP (participation; full key 305020409998): If a circle overlaps the player for half a second, should one hit cost one life or many lives? Why?
GROUP LEARN / HOOK: Create a variable lives for ALL sprites; reset to 3 when the green flag runs. In the FallingObject script, AFTER a drop begins, use a per-drop local variable hitThisFall initially 0. Each movement step checks if touching [Player] AND hitThisFall=0; if so change lives by −1 and set hitThisFall to 1. An alternative simpler teacher-tested recipe immediately sends the FallingObject back to the top after one contact, avoiding repeat deductions. This day focuses on ONE tested method; do not stack both alternatives together. The player and falling scripts must remain separately attached. Lives is visible on the stage; when lives reaches 0, show a simple Game Over message or stop only the appropriate gameplay scripts using a modeled teacher recipe.
GROUP PRACTICE: Teacher demonstrates a single contact and compares lives 3→2 with an intentionally broken many-hit loop. Students identify where the hit gate must reset for the next fall, then explain why a reliable check is more useful than a lucky test.
DAILY MASTERY STUDENT QUESTION — FULL KEY 305020430062: A collision makes lives fall from 3 to 0 instantly because the sprites overlap for several loop checks. Explain ONE coding change to count the collision only once per falling object, and describe a test for the fix.
PINNED HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 accurate, specific and independently justified with a feasible test; 70–89 Identifies a valid one-hit-per-drop guard or immediate reset and a test that distinguishes correct versus repeated deduction; 50–69 partially correct, missing important detail or validation; below 50 insufficient/contradictory evidence. Missing/unsubmitted is a separate nonnumeric state under RTS-02.
INDEPENDENCE: The question is answerable from TODAY'S teaching and examples without requiring the actual game to work or reference to an unfinished artifact. At most ONE short typed answer field; accessible optional selections may support it. Submit through the shared capture-first two-button Form workflow; no fabricated receipt.
PERFORM / PROJECT DEVELOPMENT: Add lives and one-hit-per-drop logic by copying the teacher's displayed tested code recipe. Run at least three deliberate contacts and three misses. Verify one contact lowers lives once, a miss does not, and green flag restores 3. Save same project. If a student's script is broken, restart from the shared working checkpoint instead of deleting earlier progress.
CREATIVE STUDIO (one required participation zone, separate Xtra; student's choice using same taught tools): Sketch a life-counter icon; compare three lives versus five; write a fair-game rule a player could read.
TEKS TEMPERATURE CHECK: thumbs for today's skill plus optional specific confusion. Separate Xtra, not part of DAILY mastery or Major.
END-OF-DAY SAVED EVIDENCE: Collision costs exactly one life per drop; restart restores the counter.
NEXT DAY PREPARATION: Keep original file; do not start a second game or replace placeholder sprites until Part 2.

tabs.title: Day 5
tabs.text:
DAY 5 | DAYID 3050205 | PERFORM | Score, Challenge and Playtesting
LEARNING TARGET: I can test and refine a simple game because measurable feedback helps designers make it playable and fair.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
§126.18(c)(4)(B): Explain how worldwide trends influence the technology people develop.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm. §126.18(c)(1)(F): Explain why repeating code or steps can make an algorithm useful. §126.18(c)(2)(A): Change and rename variables, and describe the kinds of data they store.
50-MINUTE RHYTHM: 4 min Warm-Up; 13 min Group Learn with live teacher demo; 7 min Group Practice/prediction; 6 min independent DAILY evidence; 15 min project build/test; 5 min save/TEKS Temperature/Studio as appropriate. Shrink activities before rushing or making assumptions about previous class completion.
WARM-UP (participation; full key 305020509998): A game is random but impossible to win. Is randomness alone enough to make it fair?
GROUP LEARN / HOOK: The prototype now needs a simple clear objective: dodge the falling circle to earn points, survive three lives, and restart. Create a score variable for ALL sprites and set it to 0 at green flag. When an entire fall completes WITHOUT a collision, change score by 1 once before restarting the next fall; when hitThisFall=1, do not award a dodge point. Teacher supplies the correct arrangement, including how to stop scoring when lives reaches 0. Demonstrate two before/after playtests using the same 30-second duration. Industry connection: designers and QA testers describe bugs, record steps and improve a specific rule; accessible controls and new device interfaces influence game design worldwide.
GROUP PRACTICE: Teacher compares successful dodge, one hit, and restart while class predicts score/lives. Learners discuss a reported unfair spawn and select a measurable adjustment to speed or x range. Use fixed test conditions to decide whether the change improved play.
DAILY MASTERY STUDENT QUESTION — FULL KEY 305020530063: Playtesters say falling objects appear right over the player and move too fast. Propose TWO specific adjustments to make the prototype fairer and explain how you would compare the original and revised versions.
PINNED HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 accurate, specific and independently justified with a feasible test; 70–89 Offers two feasible, distinct design changes and a comparative playtest with observable success criteria; 50–69 partially correct, missing important detail or validation; below 50 insufficient/contradictory evidence. Missing/unsubmitted is a separate nonnumeric state under RTS-02.
INDEPENDENCE: The question is answerable from TODAY'S teaching and examples without requiring the actual game to work or reference to an unfinished artifact. At most ONE short typed answer field; accessible optional selections may support it. Submit through the shared capture-first two-button Form workflow; no fabricated receipt.
PERFORM / PROJECT DEVELOPMENT: Add score exactly once for a safe dodge, confirm collision/lives remain functional, write one player-instruction sentence, playtest 30 seconds twice, note one observed bug and one controlled change, then save the SAME project. Leave square/circle placeholders. This is a milestone build, not the artwork phase.
CREATIVE STUDIO (one required participation zone, separate Xtra; student's choice using same taught tools): Invent a clear score label; sketch a start-screen layout for later; calculate which falling speed feels challenging but fair.
TEKS TEMPERATURE CHECK: thumbs for today's skill plus optional specific confusion. Separate Xtra, not part of DAILY mastery or Major.
END-OF-DAY SAVED EVIDENCE: Playable prototype: player movement, falling, collision/lives, score, restart and documented test.
NEXT DAY PREPARATION: Keep original file; do not start a second game or replace placeholder sprites until Part 2.

tabs.title: Day 6 — Assessment
tabs.text:
DAY 6 | DAYID 3050206 | ASSESSMENT + EARLIER DAILY RECOVERY | Prototype Skills
LEARNING TARGET: I can explain how my playable prototype uses design choices, events, loops, variables and testing because understanding the mechanics helps me transfer what I learned.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
§126.18(c)(4)(B): Explain how worldwide trends influence the technology people develop.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm. §126.18(c)(1)(F): Explain why repeating code or steps can make an algorithm useful. §126.18(c)(2)(A): Change and rename variables, and describe the kinds of data they store.
GRADE: ONE Skyward MAJOR assignment from four separately submitted equally weighted holistic assessment sections (keys 305020639991–305020639994); no new ordinary TEKS mastery IDs. Assessment 22–27 minutes including four copy/Form transitions. Partial Study & Recall notes may be consulted; no hidden answer key.
STUDY & RECALL (no solutions): Sprite = independently programmed screen object; Stage = world; x is horizontal, y is vertical; an event starts a script; a loop repeats; a variable stores a changeable value; a condition tests a rule; random selects within a stated range; a prototype tests the simplest interaction; playtests compare a prediction with what actually happened. These are concepts, not prewritten answers to test scenarios.
INSTRUCTIONS: Read each short scenario independently, select any requested option and type concise explanations. For each section create the COMPLETE answer and use the shared Copy & Submit route to the established school Form with the exact full key. The Form receipt is not assumed until actually submitted. Unanswered fields are still copied with [Not answered] markers for recovery; don't block submission. After all four, work on previously posted weaker/missing DAILY questions in their ORIGINAL guides, not the new Major, which will be graded before next recovery.
SECTION 1 | FULL KEY 305020639991 | Understanding the Prototype
STUDENT PROMPT: A game starts with one blue square and one red circle. (A) Which should be separate sprites, and why? (B) State one design-process action you would take before decorating them.
PINNED HOLISTIC TEACHER RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 precisely explains separate sprite scripts plus deliberate prototype/test purpose; 70–89 identifies the two sprites, independent behavior and a plausible design-process action; 50–69 partially accurate but misses an important reason/action; below 50 unsupported. Grade actual submitted evidence, not effort.
Evidence: a concise constructed answer or equivalent accessible choices with at most one short typed explanation; all presented response components serialize to a single purple preview and copy-first submission. No project building during these sections.

SECTION 2 | FULL KEY 305020639992 | Events and Player Controls
STUDENT PROMPT: A player starts at x=0. (A) Predict whether changing x by +8 moves it right or left. (B) Explain which event and repeated input check would let the right arrow move it every time the game runs.
PINNED HOLISTIC TEACHER RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 accurate x-direction, green-flag reset and forever/key check with clear causal explanation; 70–89 correct direction and workable event/loop/input logic; 50–69 partly correct or missing repeated behavior; below 50 unsupported.
Evidence: a concise constructed answer or equivalent accessible choices with at most one short typed explanation; all presented response components serialize to a single purple preview and copy-first submission. No project building during these sections.

SECTION 3 | FULL KEY 305020639993 | Falling Loops and Randomness
STUDENT PROMPT: A falling object reaches y=−180. (A) Describe the reset and repeat needed for another fall. (B) Explain what changes if its top x position is chosen randomly.
PINNED HOLISTIC TEACHER RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 correctly connects y boundary, top reset, repeat/forever structure and changed starting position with a relevant gameplay consequence; 70–89 states a valid reset/repeat and explains varied x; 50–69 partial or ambiguous; below 50 unsupported.
Evidence: a concise constructed answer or equivalent accessible choices with at most one short typed explanation; all presented response components serialize to a single purple preview and copy-first submission. No project building during these sections.

SECTION 4 | FULL KEY 305020639994 | Fair Collisions and Testing
STUDENT PROMPT: A hit drains all three lives immediately, and safe dodges are never rewarded. (A) Propose one fix for repeated hit-counting and one fix for scoring successful dodges. (B) State one repeatable test showing both work.
PINNED HOLISTIC TEACHER RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 provides correct one-hit guard, one-score-per-dodge trigger and controlled repeatable test; 70–89 addresses both logic problems with a feasible observable test; 50–69 only one sound fix or weak test; below 50 unsupported.
Evidence: a concise constructed answer or equivalent accessible choices with at most one short typed explanation; all presented response components serialize to a single purple preview and copy-first submission. No project building during these sections.
TEKS TEMPERATURE: show confidence thumbs on stage/sprites, events/controls, falling/repetition, hit/score, and testing; optional precise confusion note submitted separately under 305020629999.
CREATIVE STUDIO (separate participation Xtra, key 305020620000, unlocked): choose ONE playful extension using already-known tools: name a favorite arcade prototype; sketch a clearer life display; compare two control instruction sentences. Submit what you actually tried or discovered. Do not inflate the Major.
RECOVERY WINDOW (remaining 13–18 min): consult posted Skyward Daily feedback and revisit original evidence through its original guide/key. For each question identify the weaker part, improve answer with new demonstrated understanding, and resubmit. Avoid assigning new test recovery before its grade is posted. Teacher grades assessment promptly and schedules the next genuine Major-recovery opportunity after students see exact section feedback.
PASS/READY GATE: Exact four full keys and rubrics must be pinned to JISD Collector Assessment Sections; verified clipboard/Form, offline browser and one-Major scoring route needed; no student release without Captain.

tabs.title: Day 7 — Milestone & Recovery
tabs.text:
DAY 7 | DAYID 3050207 | PROTOTYPE MILESTONE COMPLETION + MAJOR/DAILY RECOVERY
LEARNING TARGET: I can finish, test and preserve a working game prototype because designers need reliable mechanics before investing in story and artwork.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm. §126.18(c)(1)(F): Explain why repeating code or steps can make an algorithm useful. §126.18(c)(2)(A): Change and rename variables, and describe the kinds of data they store.
FIRST HALF (~25 min): Open the SAME TurboWarp project from earlier days. Confirm placeholder Player square and FallingObject circle (NO story sprites yet); green flag resets player, score=0 and lives=3; left/right input works with boundaries; circle falls from randomized x; contact costs exactly one life; safe dodge awards exactly one score; restart recovers initial state. Use the complete teacher-supported working code checkpoint for a genuine blocker; do not replace the project or attempt unrelated graphics. Play a full 30-second round, record expected versus observed result for one mechanic, fix one error, save the SAME editable project using the school's confirmed workflow, and submit the milestone by the verified teacher-designated assignment. Do NOT invent a Google Classroom URL.
SUCCESS CHECK: One repeatable playable shape prototype, clear controls, score/lives, fair hit rule and an observed test; unfinished advanced features are not required. Save a duplicate BACKUP only if school tool supports verified local export, not as a new class project. Sketch possible story themes but do NOT replace sprites until Part 2.
SECOND HALF (~25 min): Once the Day 6 MAJOR grade and per-section status are in Skyward, students locate any weaker/missing section and return to the ORIGINAL Day 6 Guide and its exact reserved section to create a clearer answer. They may also recover earlier DAILY original questions. Each stronger verified resubmission updates the SAME assignment, never an effort/participation bonus. If assessment results are not posted before this session, postpone its Major recovery opportunity rather than treating the time as completed; continue genuine earlier Daily recovery, targeted reteaching or productive project review instead.
CREATIVE STUDIO (when genuinely available): sketch an invented character that could later replace the square, identify a story world, or compare two instruction designs; this is Xtra and no new mastery key.
ASSESSMENT: NO new academic mastery question or second Major on this day. Project milestone is separate from the assessment and existing DAILY grade receipts.
NEXT PART HANDOFF: Keep this exact working game; Part 2 adds story, characters and costumes while preserving the engine.
NO STUDENT RELEASE UNTIL CAPTAIN AUTHORIZES complete QA.
